summary: Struts2 (2.3.5–2.3.31, 2.5–2.5.10) evaluates OGNL from a malformed Content-Type header via the Jakarta multipart parser, giving unauthenticated RCE.

fingerprint.detection: requests to /vpn/../vpns/ and newXML template writes under /netscaler/portal/templates.

summary: Unpatched Citrix ADC/Gateway allows a /vpn/../vpns/ path traversal that stages and then executes a template, giving unauthenticated RCE. A patch-level fingerprint.
title: Citrix ADC / Gateway — path traversal to RCE (CVE-2019-19781, Shitrix)

summary: The BIG-IP Traffic Management UI mishandles '..;/', letting an unauthenticated attacker reach an internal handler and run commands as root.

fingerprint.detection: a spooler-loaded DLL from a UNC path; event 808/spooler driver-add from a client.

summary: The Print Spooler's AddPrinterDriverEx loads a driver DLL from an attacker path as SYSTEM — local privilege escalation, or remote code execution with any domain creds.

summary: ProxyShell chains an Autodiscover SSRF, an elevated PowerShell backend and a mailbox export to drop a webshell on an unpatched Exchange server — unauthenticated RCE.

fingerprint.technique: pre-auth SSRF to authenticate as the server, then an arbitrary file write to a webshell

summary: ProxyLogon pairs a pre-auth SSRF that impersonates the Exchange server with an arbitrary file write, landing a webshell on an unpatched on-prem Exchange.
title: Microsoft Exchange — ProxyLogon SSRF+RCE (CVE-2021-26855 / 27065)

fingerprint.detection: request params naming class.module.classLoader / pattern / suffix; a new .jsp in webapps.

title: Spring MVC — Spring4Shell class-loader RCE (CVE-2022-22965)

fingerprint.detection: a request for /remote/fgt_lang?lang=/../../.../sslvpn_websession in the log.

summary: Unpatched FortiOS SSL-VPN leaks the session file — containing plaintext credentials — through a pre-auth path traversal. Harvest, then reuse.
title: Fortinet FortiOS SSL-VPN — path traversal creds leak (CVE-2018-13379)

fingerprint.detection: a request query beginning with '?-' (e.g. ?-d, ?-s) reaching php-cgi.
fingerprint.solved_via: request ?-d+allow_url_include=1+-d+auto_prepend_file=php://input and POST PHP code; php-cgi treats the query as CLI args and executes the body.
fingerprint.technique: a query string with no '=' is passed as php-cgi args, enabling -d directives

summary: php-cgi below 5.4.2/5.3.12 passes a '='-less query string as command-line arguments, so -d directives + php://input give unauthenticated RCE.
title: PHP-CGI — query-string argument injection RCE (CVE-2012-1823)

fingerprint.detection: /public/plugins/<id>/ requests with ../ traversal in the access log.
fingerprint.solved_via: request /public/plugins/<plugin>/../../../../etc/passwd (and grafana.db / grafana.ini for secrets), then decrypt data-source credentials with the config secret key.
fingerprint.technique: unauthenticated ../ traversal through the plugin public path

summary: Grafana 8.0.0–8.3.0 allows an unauthenticated path traversal through the plugin static path — read /etc/passwd, grafana.db and grafana.ini to pivot on secrets.
title: Grafana — plugin path traversal / LFI (CVE-2021-43798)

fingerprint.detection: a SOAP POST to /wls-wsat/ carrying <java><void>/ProcessBuilder XML.
fingerprint.solved_via: POST a crafted XMLDecoder workContext to /wls-wsat/CoordinatorPortType for RCE; T3 on 7001 is the alternative vector. Confirm the endpoint responds first.
fingerprint.technique: XMLDecoder deserialization via the wls-wsat endpoint (or the T3 protocol)

summary: WebLogic's wls-wsat endpoint deserialises attacker XML via XMLDecoder, giving unauthenticated RCE; the T3 protocol on 7001 is a second path.
title: Oracle WebLogic — T3 / XMLDecoder deserialization RCE (CVE-2017-10271)

fingerprint.detection: index.php?target= with a traversal / double-encoded ? in the query.
fingerprint.solved_via: run a query so its result lands in the session file, then include that session file via ?target=db_sql.php%253f/../../../../session to execute PHP you controlled.
fingerprint.technique: the target parameter of index.php includes an arbitrary local file

summary: phpMyAdmin 4.8.0/4.8.1 includes the 'target' parameter without proper validation, so a traversal (double-encoded ?) turns an LFI into RCE via the PHP session file.
title: phpMyAdmin 4.8.0–4.8.1 — LFI to RCE (CVE-2018-12613)

fingerprint.detection: sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell',1 then EXEC xp_cmdshell in the SQL audit log.
fingerprint.solved_via: with sa (or a login in sysadmin), enable xp_cmdshell via sp_configure and run OS commands as the SQL service account. impacket-mssqlclient, then enable_xp_cmdshell.
fingerprint.technique: enable and call xp_cmdshell as a privileged SQL login to run OS commands

summary: A privileged MSSQL login can enable xp_cmdshell and run OS commands as the SQL service account — the standard pivot from weak sa creds to a shell.
title: MSSQL — xp_cmdshell command execution with sa/db creds

fingerprint.detection: a burst of SNMP GET/GETNEXT with 'public'/'private' from one host on UDP 161.
fingerprint.solved_via: walk the MIB with a default community to pull processes, users, listening ports, installed software, and sometimes credentials in process args. snmpwalk / snmp-check.
fingerprint.technique: read the MIB with a guessable community string (public/private) over UDP 161

summary: A device answering SNMP with a default community string (public/private) leaks the whole MIB — processes, ports, users, and command-line credentials.
title: SNMP — public community string enumeration

fingerprint.detection: COPY ... FROM PROGRAM or CREATE FUNCTION ... LANGUAGE c in the postgres log.
fingerprint.solved_via: as a superuser DB role, COPY a table FROM PROGRAM '<cmd>' to run OS commands as the postgres user; the C-language UDF is the alternative. psql with captured creds.
fingerprint.technique: a superuser role runs OS commands via COPY ... FROM PROGRAM (or a C UDF)

summary: A PostgreSQL superuser role can execute OS commands via COPY FROM PROGRAM (or a C UDF), running as the postgres system user — the standard DB-to-shell pivot.
title: PostgreSQL — RCE via COPY PROGRAM / UDF as superuser (CVE-2019-9193)

fingerprint.detection: a POST to /password_change.cgi with shell metacharacters in the 'old' field.
fingerprint.solved_via: POST to /password_change.cgi with a pipe/backtick in the old-password field when password expiry is enabled; it runs as root. metasploit webmin_backdoor.
fingerprint.technique: command injection in the password_change.cgi 'old' field (tainted release)

summary: A tainted Webmin release (1.882–1.920) has a command injection in password_change.cgi, giving unauthenticated RCE as root when expiry is enabled.
title: Webmin 1.882–1.920 — password_change backdoor RCE (CVE-2019-15107)

fingerprint.detection: an over-long / serialized-object User-Agent, then odd session deserialization.
fingerprint.solved_via: send a PHP-object payload in the User-Agent (or X-Forwarded-For); it is persisted to the session and unserialized on the next request, executing your gadget.
fingerprint.technique: a crafted User-Agent is stored then unserialized from the session, giving RCE

summary: Joomla before 3.4.6 stores the User-Agent into the session and unserializes it, so a PHP object-injection payload in that header yields unauthenticated RCE.
title: Joomla 1.5–3.4.5 — User-Agent object injection RCE (CVE-2015-8562)

fingerprint.detection: a _search request carrying a script with java.lang.Runtime / getRuntime in it.
fingerprint.solved_via: POST a _search with a script_fields Groovy expression that reaches java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(); runs as the elasticsearch user on 9200.
fingerprint.technique: a script query escapes the Groovy sandbox to run Java Runtime.exec

summary: Elasticsearch before 1.3.8/1.4.3 lets a Groovy script query escape the sandbox and call Runtime.exec — unauthenticated RCE on the 9200 API.
title: Elasticsearch ≤ 1.3.7 — Groovy sandbox bypass RCE (CVE-2015-1427)

fingerprint.detection: AS-REQ without pre-auth (event 4768) for several users from one source.
fingerprint.solved_via: enumerate accounts without pre-auth, request their AS-REP encrypted with the user's key, and crack offline. GetNPUsers.py; hashcat -m 18200.
fingerprint.technique: request an AS-REP for accounts with 'Do not require Kerberos preauth' and crack it

summary: Accounts flagged 'do not require pre-auth' hand out an AS-REP that anyone can request and crack offline — no valid creds needed to roast.
title: Active Directory — AS-REP roasting (no Kerberos pre-auth)

fingerprint.detection: DRSUAPI GetNCChanges (replication) from a host that is NOT a domain controller.
fingerprint.solved_via: from an account with replication rights (Domain/Enterprise Admin, or a delegated ACL), replicate the krbtgt and target hashes. secretsdump -just-dc / mimikatz lsadump::dcsync.
fingerprint.technique: use replication rights (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All) to pull every NTLM hash

summary: With replication rights, an attacker asks a DC to replicate account secrets — the krbtgt hash and every NTLM hash — without touching LSASS.
title: Active Directory — DCSync (replicate domain secrets)

fingerprint.detection: a machine account renamed to a DC name; a TGS request where account name != SPN.
fingerprint.solved_via: with rights to create a computer (default MachineAccountQuota=10), create one, clear its SPN, rename it to a DC's sAMAccountName, request a TGT then an S4U2self ticket as administrator. noPac.py / sam_the_admin.
fingerprint.technique: rename a machine account to a DC name so a TGS is issued for the DC's context

summary: A KDC confusion between sAMAccountName and SPN lets a low-priv user who can add a computer escalate straight to Domain Admin on an unpatched DC.
title: Active Directory — noPac / sAMAccountName spoofing (CVE-2021-42278 / 42287)

fingerprint.detection: a coercion trigger (MS-RPRN/EFSRPC) then a DC TGT appearing on a member host.
fingerprint.solved_via: on a host with unconstrained delegation, coerce a DC (printerbug/PetitPotam) to authenticate, capture the DC's TGT from memory, then DCSync. Rubeus monitor.
fingerprint.technique: coerce a privileged host to authenticate; its TGT is cached on the delegating host

summary: A host trusted for unconstrained delegation caches the TGT of anything that authenticates to it — coerce a DC and you own the domain.
title: Active Directory — unconstrained delegation TGT capture

fingerprint.detection: a write to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity, then S4U ticket requests.
fingerprint.solved_via: with GenericWrite/WriteDACL over a computer, add a computer you control to its msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOf, then S4U2self+S4U2proxy to get a service ticket as any user. rbcd.py + getST.
fingerprint.technique: write msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on a target to impersonate via S4U

summary: GenericWrite over a computer object lets you set RBCD to a machine you control and then impersonate any user to that computer's services.
title: Active Directory — resource-based constrained delegation abuse (RBCD)

fingerprint.detection: EFSRPC coercion to the DC, NTLM relayed to /certsrv, a DC-template cert issued.
fingerprint.solved_via: start ntlmrelayx targeting http://<ca>/certsrv (ESC8), coerce the DC with PetitPotam; the relayed DC machine auth requests a cert you then use to get the DC's TGT and DCSync.
fingerprint.technique: coerce DC auth (EFSRPC) and relay NTLM to the ADCS web enrollment for a DC cert

summary: If ADCS web enrollment accepts NTLM (ESC8), relay a coerced DC's authentication to it for a DC certificate — then authenticate as the DC and take the domain.
title: Active Directory — PetitPotam coercion + ADCS ESC8 NTLM relay

fingerprint.detection: SYSVOL reads of Groups.xml carrying a cpassword attribute.
fingerprint.solved_via: as any domain user, read Groups.xml (and services/scheduledtasks) from SYSVOL, then decrypt cPassword with the published AES key. Get-GPPPassword / gpp-decrypt.
fingerprint.technique: decrypt the AES-encrypted cPassword left in Group Policy Preference XML on SYSVOL

summary: Old Group Policy Preferences stored credentials as a cPassword encrypted with a static, published AES key — any domain user can read SYSVOL and decrypt them.
title: Active Directory — GPP cPassword in SYSVOL (MS14-025, CVE-2014-1812)

fingerprint.detection: LDAP reads of ms-Mcs-AdmPwd across many computer objects from one principal.
fingerprint.solved_via: if your user/group can read the LAPS attribute on a host, pull its rotating local administrator password and log in. netexec --laps / pyLAPS / ldapsearch.
fingerprint.technique: read ms-Mcs-AdmPwd on a computer object when your principal has the ACL

summary: LAPS randomises each host's local admin password but stores it in AD; whoever holds the read ACL on a computer object gets that host's admin password.
title: Active Directory — LAPS local admin password read

fingerprint.detection: NTLM logons (event 4624 type 3) for an account from an unusual source host.
fingerprint.solved_via: reuse a captured NTLM hash to authenticate to hosts where that account is local admin, no cracking needed. netexec -H, psexec.py -hashes, evil-winrm -H.
fingerprint.technique: authenticate with an NTLM hash instead of a password over SMB/WMI/WinRM

summary: NTLM authentication needs the hash, not the plaintext — a dumped hash moves laterally to every host where that account has admin rights.
title: Active Directory — pass-the-hash lateral movement

fingerprint.detection: a TGT with an anomalous lifetime / a user that does not exist; RC4 where AES is expected.
fingerprint.solved_via: with the krbtgt NTLM/AES key (from DCSync), forge a TGT as any principal — total, durable domain access. ticketer.py / mimikatz kerberos::golden.
fingerprint.technique: forge a TGT with the krbtgt hash to impersonate any user indefinitely

summary: The krbtgt key signs every TGT, so possessing it lets you forge tickets for any user — the ultimate domain persistence until krbtgt is rotated twice.
title: Active Directory — Golden ticket persistence (krbtgt)

fingerprint.detection: mongod connections from external hosts with no auth handshake on 27017.
fingerprint.solved_via: connect with no credentials, list databases and collections, dump application data and any stored credentials. mongosh / mongo --host.
fingerprint.technique: connect to an open mongod (27017) with no auth and read every database

summary: A MongoDB bound to a reachable interface with auth disabled exposes every database to anyone — application data and often plaintext or hashed credentials.
title: MongoDB — unauthenticated access

fingerprint.detection: memcached stats/get from external hosts on 11211; large UDP responses.
fingerprint.solved_via: dump cached keys/items to harvest session tokens and application secrets; the same open UDP service is a reflection/amplification vector. stats items + get.
fingerprint.technique: read cached items over 11211 with no auth (and UDP reflection risk)

summary: An exposed Memcached serves its entire cache — session data, tokens, query results — to anyone, and its UDP port doubles as a DDoS amplifier.
title: Memcached — unauthenticated data / amplification

fingerprint.detection: a _users PUT with duplicate JSON keys, then a _config/query_servers write.
fingerprint.solved_via: create an admin via the duplicate-'roles' JSON quirk (12635), then set a query_server to an OS command and trigger it (12636) for RCE as couchdb.
fingerprint.technique: JSON duplicate-key parser mismatch grants admin, then _config query_server runs code

summary: CouchDB before 2.1.1 mishandles duplicate JSON keys to make an admin, then the query-server config turns that admin into unauthenticated RCE.
title: Apache CouchDB — privilege escalation + query-server RCE (CVE-2017-12635 / 12636)

fingerprint.detection: INTO DUMPFILE writes into the plugin dir, then CREATE FUNCTION ... sys_exec.
fingerprint.solved_via: as a privileged DB user, write lib_mysqludf_sys into the plugin directory and CREATE FUNCTION sys_exec to run OS commands as the mysql user. Weak root is the way in.
fingerprint.technique: load a shared-object UDF (sys_exec/do_system) with FILE/INSERT into a plugin dir

summary: A MySQL user with FILE privilege can drop a UDF library into the plugin directory and register sys_exec, running OS commands as the mysql service account.
title: MySQL — UDF command execution as the mysql user

fingerprint.detection: RMI registry lookups then an MLet loading a remote MBean JAR.
fingerprint.solved_via: connect to an unauthenticated JMX service, register an MLet that fetches a malicious MBean from your HTTP server, and invoke it for code execution. metasploit java_jmx_server.
fingerprint.technique: an open JMX/RMI registry lets you load a malicious MBean (MLet) for RCE

summary: An unauthenticated JMX/RMI endpoint accepts an MLet that loads an attacker MBean from a URL — direct remote code execution in the JVM.
title: Java JMX / RMI — unauthenticated MLet RCE

fingerprint.detection: RAKP message-1 requests for many usernames on UDP 623.
fingerprint.solved_via: request a RAKP message for a valid/guessed username; the BMC returns a salted SHA1 HMAC you crack offline, then log into the management interface. ipmitool / metasploit.
fingerprint.technique: the RAKP protocol returns a crackable HMAC of any user's password pre-auth

summary: The IPMI 2.0 RAKP handshake hands out a crackable HMAC of the requested user's password before authentication — dump, crack, and own the BMC.
title: IPMI 2.0 — RAKP authentication hash dump (CVE-2013-4786)

fingerprint.detection: VNC connections from external hosts on 5900+; repeated auth attempts.
fingerprint.solved_via: scan 5900-5901 for VNC, connect with no auth where enabled, or crack the short VNC password (max 8 chars) offline / by spray. vncviewer / hydra.
fingerprint.technique: connect to a VNC service with no auth or a short/guessable password

summary: VNC is often left with no authentication or an 8-character password, giving an interactive desktop session to whoever connects.
title: VNC — no-auth / weak password access

fingerprint.detection: a burst of malformed SSH auth requests across many usernames.
fingerprint.solved_via: send a crafted public-key auth request; valid usernames respond measurably slower, so you enumerate accounts to feed a spray. Then target weak creds.
fingerprint.technique: a malformed auth packet takes longer for valid users, leaking valid names

summary: OpenSSH before 7.8 leaks whether a username exists through an auth-timing side channel — enumerate valid accounts, then spray.
title: OpenSSH — username enumeration timing (CVE-2018-15473)

fingerprint.detection: an FTP login with user 'anonymous'; uploads to a web-served path.
fingerprint.solved_via: log in anonymous, download everything for creds/config; if a directory is writable and web-served, upload a shell. nmap ftp-anon confirms it.
fingerprint.technique: log in as anonymous and read (or write) served files

summary: Anonymous FTP hands out whatever it serves — often config, backups and credentials, and a writable web-served dir turns it into a webshell drop.
title: FTP — anonymous access

fingerprint.detection: LDAP searches with an empty bind DN returning large result sets.
fingerprint.solved_via: anonymous-bind and dump users, groups and description fields — passwords are frequently left in description/info. ldapsearch -x, windapsearch.
fingerprint.technique: bind with no credentials and read directory objects (users, descriptions)

summary: An LDAP/AD directory permitting anonymous bind leaks the user list and often credentials stashed in description or info attributes.
title: LDAP — anonymous bind enumeration

fingerprint.detection: repeated VRFY/EXPN or RCPT-TO probes across many local-parts.
fingerprint.solved_via: enumerate valid users via VRFY/RCPT differential responses to feed a spray, and test whether the server relays mail for anyone. smtp-user-enum / nmap.
fingerprint.technique: probe VRFY/EXPN/RCPT-TO responses to distinguish valid mailboxes

summary: An SMTP server that answers VRFY/EXPN or differentiates RCPT-TO responses leaks valid usernames, and an open relay lets you send mail as anyone.
title: SMTP — user enumeration (VRFY / EXPN / RCPT) + open relay

fingerprint.detection: an unexpected write to /etc/passwd or a SUID binary; a new uid-0 shell.
fingerprint.solved_via: on kernels 5.8 to ~5.16.11, overwrite a root-owned read-only file (drop the root password hash, or hijack a SUID binary) to get root. Public one-shot PoC.
fingerprint.technique: a pipe page-cache flaw overwrites read-only files, incl. /etc/passwd or a SUID binary

summary: DirtyPipe lets an unprivileged process overwrite pages of read-only files via the pipe subsystem — patch /etc/passwd or a SUID helper for instant root.
title: Linux kernel — DirtyPipe arbitrary file overwrite (CVE-2022-0847)

fingerprint.detection: a modified SUID binary / passwd; a new root account with no shadow entry.
fingerprint.solved_via: on older kernels, race the COW mapping to overwrite a SUID binary or /etc/passwd for root. Use a PoC variant that matches the box (dirtyc0w / pokemon).
fingerprint.technique: a copy-on-write race lets an unprivileged user write to read-only mappings

summary: Dirty COW races the copy-on-write handler to write read-only memory mappings, giving local root on unpatched kernels (fixed ~4.8.3).
title: Linux kernel — Dirty COW race condition (CVE-2016-5195)

fingerprint.detection: sudoedit invoked with an escaped/oversized argument; a crash then a root shell.
fingerprint.solved_via: on sudo 1.8.2-1.9.5p1, run the public exploit; it corrupts the heap for local root without any sudoers entry. Match the PoC to the libc/sudo build.
fingerprint.technique: a heap buffer overflow via sudoedit -s with a trailing backslash, no sudo rights needed

summary: Baron Samedit is a heap overflow reachable by ANY local user (no sudo permission needed) on sudo 1.8.2-1.9.5p1 — reliable local root.
title: sudo — Baron Samedit heap overflow (CVE-2021-3156)

fingerprint.detection: a container started with -v /:/... or --privileged from a low-priv user.
fingerprint.solved_via: if you can reach /var/run/docker.sock (docker group, or a mounted socket), run a container with the host / bind-mounted and chroot in as root. docker run -v /:/mnt.
fingerprint.technique: talk to the Docker daemon to run a privileged container mounting the host root

summary: Access to the Docker socket is root-equivalent: launch a container that mounts the host filesystem and read/write anything, or add yourself to sudoers.
title: Linux — writable Docker socket / docker group to root

fingerprint.detection: lxc init/config device add security.privileged=true from a low-priv user.
fingerprint.solved_via: as an lxd/lxc group member, import a small image, start a privileged container with the host disk mounted, and read/write it as root. The alpine-builder trick.
fingerprint.technique: an lxd-group member launches a privileged container mounting the host filesystem

summary: The lxd group is root-equivalent: a privileged container with the host path mounted gives full read/write to the host as root.
title: Linux — lxd/lxc group to root

fingerprint.detection: a new SUID-root binary appearing on an NFS export; mounts from an odd host.
fingerprint.solved_via: mount the no_root_squash export as root on your box, drop a SUID-root shell into it, then run it on the target as a normal user for root. showmount -e to find it.
fingerprint.technique: a share exported with no_root_squash lets a remote root create a SUID-root binary

summary: An NFS export with no_root_squash trusts remote root, so you write a SUID-root binary from your machine and execute it on the target to escalate.
title: Linux — NFS no_root_squash SUID drop

fingerprint.detection: a privileged process exec'ing a binary from a user-writable/unusual PATH entry.
fingerprint.solved_via: find a SUID/sudo binary that invokes another command without an absolute path, put a malicious version earlier in PATH, and run it. strings/ltrace reveal the call.
fingerprint.technique: a privileged program calls a command by name; you prepend a writable dir to PATH

summary: A SUID or sudo-run program that calls a helper by bare name (e.g. `service`, `cat`) trusts $PATH — plant your own helper earlier in PATH to run code as root.
title: Linux — PATH hijack of a SUID/sudo program calling a relative binary

fingerprint.detection: LD_PRELOAD set on a sudo invocation; a .so loaded from /tmp by a root process.
fingerprint.solved_via: if `sudo -l` shows env_keep+=LD_PRELOAD, compile a .so with a root-shell constructor and preload it while running any allowed sudo command.
fingerprint.technique: sudoers keeps LD_PRELOAD; a malicious .so runs as root when you sudo a command

summary: A sudoers `env_keep += LD_PRELOAD` lets you preload an attacker library into any sudo-allowed command, running your constructor as root.
title: Linux — LD_PRELOAD via sudo env_keep to root

fingerprint.detection: files named '--checkpoint-action=...' or '-e sh' in a cron-processed directory.
fingerprint.solved_via: in a directory a root cron globs (e.g. `tar cf a.tar *`), create files named like options (--checkpoint / --checkpoint-action=exec=sh) so the glob smuggles a command.
fingerprint.technique: a root job using a shell wildcard treats attacker-named files as command options

summary: A root cron that runs `tar`/`rsync`/`chown` with a `*` glob will expand attacker-named files into command-line options — turning file names into code execution as root.
title: Linux — wildcard injection in a root cron (tar / rsync / chown)

fingerprint.detection: requests to /actuator/env, /heapdump, /jolokia from external hosts.
fingerprint.solved_via: pull /actuator/env, /actuator/heapdump (carve credentials/tokens) and, where jolokia or a writable env property is exposed, chain to RCE. Enumerate the actuators first.
fingerprint.technique: unauthenticated /actuator endpoints leak secrets or reach code exec (jolokia/env)

summary: Exposed Spring Boot Actuator endpoints leak configuration and a full heap dump (mine it for secrets), and jolokia/env-write can be chained to code execution.
title: Spring Boot Actuator — exposed management endpoints

fingerprint.detection: POSTs to _ignition/execute-solution with makeViewVariableOptionalSolution.
fingerprint.solved_via: hit the Ignition solution endpoint to poison the laravel.log via phar/file manipulation, then include it for code execution. Confirm debug mode + Ignition first.
fingerprint.technique: with APP_DEBUG=true, the Ignition error page allows log-file poisoning to RCE

summary: A Laravel app left with APP_DEBUG=true and a vulnerable Ignition version allows unauthenticated RCE by poisoning and then including the log file.
title: Laravel — Ignition debug-mode RCE (CVE-2021-3129)

fingerprint.detection: a ${script:} / ${url:} / ${dns:} string in a parameter; egress DNS/HTTP.
fingerprint.solved_via: if user input reaches StringSubstitutor default interpolation (Commons Text 1.5-1.9), send ${script:javascript:...} to execute. Prove ${dns://} callback first.
fingerprint.technique: a ${script:...} / ${url:...} / ${dns:...} interpolator evaluates attacker input

summary: Commons Text 1.5-1.9 enables dangerous string interpolators by default, so input flowing into StringSubstitutor can carry ${script:...} for code execution.
title: Apache Commons Text — Text4Shell interpolation RCE (CVE-2022-42889)

fingerprint.detection: POSTs to /CFIDE or a .cfc endpoint with an AMF/deserialization payload.
fingerprint.solved_via: hit the vulnerable CFC/AMF path to read arbitrary files (config with credentials) and, chained, execute code. nuclei template confirms; then escalate.
fingerprint.technique: an improper-access-control deserialization in the CFC endpoint enables file read + RCE

summary: ColdFusion 2018/2021 mishandles a deserialization in the component endpoint, giving unauthenticated arbitrary file read and, chained, remote code execution.
title: Adobe ColdFusion — deserialization file read / RCE (CVE-2023-26360)

fingerprint.detection: access to /app?service=page/SetupCompleted then a script save/enable in the admin.
fingerprint.solved_via: use the SetupCompleted auth bypass to gain admin, enable the print-script feature, and run a script for code execution as the PaperCut service. nuclei confirms.
fingerprint.technique: an authentication bypass reaches the admin, then user/device scripting runs code

summary: Unpatched PaperCut lets an attacker bypass authentication to the admin console and use the built-in scripting to execute code as SYSTEM/root.
title: PaperCut NG/MF — auth bypass to scripting RCE (CVE-2023-27350)

fingerprint.detection: an unauthenticated token creation on /app/rest, then a plugin upload.
fingerprint.solved_via: abuse the RememberMe/RPC path to mint an admin token, then upload a malicious plugin or use the debug process runner to execute code on the server. PoC/metasploit.
fingerprint.technique: an unauth request creates an admin access token, then debug/agent features run code

summary: TeamCity before 2023.05.4 lets an unauthenticated attacker create an admin API token and pivot to code execution on the CI server (and its secrets).
title: JetBrains TeamCity — auth bypass to admin token RCE (CVE-2023-42793)

fingerprint.detection: requests with requirePasswordChange=Y to /webtools/control and XML-RPC gadget POSTs.
fingerprint.solved_via: use the requirePasswordChange auth bypass to reach the XML-RPC endpoint and send a ysoserial gadget for RCE. nuclei confirms; PoC chains the two CVEs.
fingerprint.technique: an empty/invalid credential bypasses auth on the XML-RPC endpoint, reaching deserialization

summary: OFBiz before 18.12.11 can be reached unauthenticated via an auth-bypass parameter, exposing an XML-RPC deserialization for remote code execution.
title: Apache OFBiz — auth bypass + SSRF/deserialization RCE (CVE-2023-51467 / 49070)

fingerprint.detection: requests to /ui/h5-vsan/rest/proxy/service with a serialized payload.
fingerprint.solved_via: hit the vropspluginui/vSAN endpoint that lacks auth to execute code as root on the vCenter appliance. nuclei/PoC confirms; then take the appliance.
fingerprint.technique: the vSAN Health plugin is exposed unauthenticated, reaching a code-exec endpoint

summary: vCenter Server exposes the vSAN Health plugin without authentication, giving remote code execution as root on the appliance — a crown-jewel target.
title: VMware vCenter — vSAN plugin unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2021-21985)

fingerprint.detection: remote_agent.php requests with a spoofed X-Forwarded-For and shell metachars.
fingerprint.solved_via: spoof X-Forwarded-For to a known host to bypass auth on remote_agent.php, then inject into the poller_id/host parameters for command execution as the web user.
fingerprint.technique: remote_agent.php auth bypass (spoofed X-Forwarded-For) + poller command injection

summary: Cacti 1.2.22 and earlier let an unauthenticated attacker reach remote_agent.php via an X-Forwarded-For bypass and inject OS commands through the poller.
title: Cacti — unauthenticated command injection (CVE-2022-46169)

fingerprint.detection: a query string containing invokefunction / call_user_func_array / \think\app.
fingerprint.solved_via: request index.php?s=index/\think\app/invokefunction with call_user_func_array to run system(). One GET is often enough; nuclei confirms the version/route.
fingerprint.technique: the framework's routing allows calling arbitrary functions via s/_method parameters

summary: ThinkPHP 5.x routing lets an unauthenticated attacker invoke arbitrary PHP functions through the s/_method parameters — a one-request RCE.
title: ThinkPHP 5.x — invokefunction RCE (CVE-2018-20062)

fingerprint.detection: xmlrpc.php system.multicall bursts; /wp-json/wp/v2/users reads; odd plugin uploads.
fingerprint.solved_via: enumerate usernames (?author=, /wp-json/wp/v2/users), brute-force via XML-RPC multicall (amplified), then find a vulnerable plugin/theme for upload or RCE. wpscan.
fingerprint.technique: enumerate authors, brute via xmlrpc system.multicall, then a vulnerable plugin -> RCE

summary: WordPress leaks usernames via the REST/author routes, XML-RPC multicall amplifies brute-forcing, and the real RCE almost always comes from a vulnerable plugin/theme.
title: WordPress — user enumeration + XML-RPC brute / plugin RCE

fingerprint.detection: __schema introspection queries; a single request with many aliased fields.
fingerprint.solved_via: run introspection to map every query/mutation, look for authz-missing fields and object-id arguments (IDOR), and use aliased batched queries to amplify or brute. graphw00f/inql.
fingerprint.technique: dump the schema via introspection, then abuse batching/aliases for DoS and IDOR

summary: An exposed GraphQL endpoint with introspection on hands you the full schema; from there, missing per-field authorization (IDOR) and alias batching (brute/DoS) are the common wins.
title: GraphQL — introspection, batching abuse and alias-based IDOR

fingerprint.detection: a POST to mboximport with a zip containing ../ entries, then a new .jsp.
fingerprint.solved_via: upload a zip whose entries traverse out of the import dir to drop a JSP webshell under the web root (37042 removes the auth requirement). Confirm the version first.
fingerprint.technique: an admin/unauth mboximport accepts a zip with traversal, writing a webshell

summary: Zimbra's mboximport unpacks an attacker zip without sanitising entry paths, so a traversal writes a webshell into the web root — unauthenticated with the 37042 bypass.
title: Zimbra Collaboration — mboximport path traversal RCE (CVE-2022-27925 / 37042)

fingerprint.detection: a MAIL FROM address containing ';' / backticks in the maillog, and an unexpected child process parented by the smtpd delivery path.
fingerprint.solved_via: the smtp_mailaddr parser accepts a crafted local-part; a ';command;' rides the MAIL FROM into execution when the message is delivered. Speak SMTP by hand or use the public PoC; the banner (OpenSMTPD) and version gate it.
fingerprint.technique: shell metacharacters in the MAIL FROM local-part run as the mail user (or root)

summary: OpenSMTPD's default install (<=6.6.1p1) mishandles the MAIL FROM local-part, so a ';cmd;' there executes on delivery — a mail-service foothold from an open 25/tcp.
title: OpenSMTPD — MAIL FROM local-part command injection (CVE-2020-7247)

fingerprint.detection: 4506/tcp reachable externally, _send_pub / wheel calls with no prior auth, and salt jobs originating from an unknown source in the master log.
fingerprint.solved_via: the salt-master ZeroMQ request server (4506/tcp) exposes _prep_auth_info and wheel functions without auth, so you recover the root key and push a command to any minion — or read/write files via the wheel. Public PoC keys off the version.
fingerprint.technique: unauthenticated ClearFuncs on the master's request server runs commands as root

summary: salt-master <=3000.1 lets an unauthenticated client call privileged ClearFuncs on 4506/tcp, recovering the root key and running commands on the master or its minions.
title: SaltStack salt-master — auth bypass to root RCE (CVE-2020-11651/-11652)

fingerprint.detection: a JSESSIONID containing '../' path segments, and a Tomcat worker deserialising a session file from outside the configured store.
fingerprint.solved_via: when PersistentManager+FileStore is enabled and you can drop a file, upload a ysoserial gadget then send JSESSIONID=../../../../path/to/file (no .session), and Tomcat deserialises it into RCE. Needs a file-write primitive first.
fingerprint.technique: a JSESSIONID pointing at an attacker-written session file triggers deserialization

summary: Tomcat 7/8/9/10-M with PersistentManager FileStore deserialises a session file named by JSESSIONID, so a path-traversal cookie pointed at an uploaded ysoserial payload is RCE — the classic 'upload + cookie' Tomcat chain.
title: Apache Tomcat — PersistentManager FileStore deserialization (CVE-2020-9484)

fingerprint.detection: a POST to /solr/<core>/config toggling params.resource.loader.enabled, followed by a wt=velocity query containing Runtime.getRuntime().exec.
fingerprint.solved_via: enable the params resource loader on a core via the config API, then request a wt=velocity response whose template body is a Java one-liner — Solr renders it and executes. Two-to-three HTTP requests, no auth on an exposed core.
fingerprint.technique: params.resource.loader.enabled lets a Velocity template in wt=velocity run code

summary: Solr 5.0-8.3.1 will render a Velocity template supplied in a wt=velocity query once the params resource loader is enabled via the config API — an unauth path to code exec on an exposed core (often behind an 8983/tcp or a tunnelled port).
title: Apache Solr — VelocityResponseWriter template RCE (CVE-2019-17558)

fingerprint.detection: a POST to /webtools/control/xmlrpc with a <serializable> element, and a java process spawning a shell from the OFBiz worker.
fingerprint.solved_via: POST a crafted XML-RPC call to /webtools/control/xmlrpc; the ROME/serializable gadget in the payload deserialises to RCE. ysoserial builds the gadget; the version gates it. (Distinct from the later 2023-51467 auth bypass already in KB.)
fingerprint.technique: an unauthenticated XML-RPC endpoint deserialises an untrusted <serializable> arg

summary: OFBiz <=17.12.03 deserialises an untrusted argument in its unauthenticated XML-RPC handler, so a ROME gadget POSTed to /webtools/control/xmlrpc is RCE.
title: Apache OFBiz — XML-RPC deserialization RCE (CVE-2020-9496)

fingerprint.detection: graph_realtime.php requests carrying SQL syntax in graph_start, and cmd-shaped poller entries in the Cacti log.
fingerprint.solved_via: the 'graph_start'/action parameters of graph_realtime.php are not sanitised; a UNION/stacked payload injects into the query and, via Cacti's poller/exec path, reaches OS commands. Needs a low-priv Cacti login (often from reused creds).
fingerprint.technique: an authenticated SQLi in graph_realtime.php reaches command execution

summary: Cacti <=1.2.12 exposes an authenticated SQL injection in graph_realtime.php that chains to command execution through the poller — a foothold once you have any Cacti account, which password-reuse often supplies.
title: Cacti — graph_realtime.php SQL injection (CVE-2020-14295)

fingerprint.detection: a cupsd.conf ErrorLog directive pointed outside /var/log, and a config change from the CUPS admin interface immediately before a sensitive-file read.
fingerprint.solved_via: with CUPS admin rights (lpadmin group / SNMP-leaked creds), set the ErrorLog directive to /etc/shadow via the config API, trigger an error, and read the log through the web UI — arbitrary file read as the cupsd user (root).
fingerprint.technique: a printer-admin points cupsd's ErrorLog at a target file, then reads it back

summary: CUPS <=1.6.1 lets a print admin repoint the ErrorLog directive at any file and read it back through the interface — a root file read (e.g. /etc/shadow) from printer admin creds, which the JetDirect/SNMP path often leaks.
title: CUPS — admin-set ErrorLog arbitrary file read (CVE-2012-5519)

fingerprint.detection: SNMP GETs walking device OIDs from an unexpected host, and PJL FSDOWNLOAD/FSUPLOAD traffic on 9100/tcp.
fingerprint.solved_via: an HP-style printer exposes its admin password through an SNMP OID (public community) or lets PRET talk PJL on 9100 to read NVRAM / filesystem. That credential is then reused against telnet/CUPS/SSH — the printer is the pivot.
fingerprint.technique: read the printer's stored credential over SNMP or via PJL/PRET on 9100/tcp

summary: An old network printer hands its stored password to anyone who reads the right SNMP OID with the public community, or who speaks PJL on 9100 via PRET — and that password is reused elsewhere, making the printer the entry point.
title: Network printer (9100/PJL + SNMP) — leak the device password

fingerprint.detection: a SET GLOBAL wsrep_provider / wsrep_notify_cmd to a non-standard path, and mysqld loading a shared object from a world-writable directory.
fingerprint.solved_via: with a MariaDB login carrying SET GLOBAL rights, point wsrep_provider (or wsrep_notify_cmd) at a malicious shared object; when the Galera provider reloads it executes as the mysql user. Needs DB creds — password reuse commonly supplies them.
fingerprint.technique: a DB user sets wsrep_provider to an attacker .so, which loads on the next restart

summary: MariaDB's wsrep_provider (Galera) accepts an arbitrary library path from a privileged DB session; a malicious .so loads as the mysql user on reload — a DB-creds-to-RCE step that pairs naturally with a leaked MySQL password.
title: MariaDB/MySQL — wsrep_provider library-load RCE (CVE-2021-27928)

fingerprint.detection: RAKP message-2 responses to unsolicited 623/udp requests, and offline cracking is invisible to the target.
fingerprint.solved_via: the IPMI 2.0 RAKP handshake hands back an HMAC-SHA1 over a known nonce for any valid account (often the default 'admin'/'ADMIN') before auth completes; crack it offline for the BMC password, which is reused into the OS or a management app.
fingerprint.technique: the RAKP protocol returns a crackable HMAC for any requested username

summary: An IPMI 2.0 BMC on 623/udp leaks a crackable RAKP HMAC for any username, so the BMC password falls to an offline crack and is then reused into Zabbix/SSH/OS — a classic management-plane foothold.
title: IPMI/BMC (623/udp) — RAKP authentication hash leak

fingerprint.detection: an import/mirror URL targeting localhost:6379, CRLF bytes in the import request, and a Sidekiq job executing from an unexpected source.
fingerprint.solved_via: the repo-mirror/import feature can be pointed at 127.0.0.1:6379 (SSRF), and CRLF in the payload smuggles Redis commands that queue a malicious Sidekiq/Resque job — GitLab deserialises it into RCE as git. Version-gated to 11.4.7 and below.
fingerprint.technique: a project-import SSRF plus CRLF injection writes a Resque job into local Redis

summary: GitLab <=11.4.7 chains an import SSRF with CRLF injection to write a job into local Redis, which GitLab runs as code — a foothold that lands you inside the GitLab container (then often a Docker escape).
title: GitLab — SSRF + CRLF into Redis for RCE (CVE-2018-19571/-19585)

fingerprint.detection: a modeline containing 'fde=' / 'fdm=expr' / 'source!' in a file dropped into a watched or shared directory, and a shell child of a vim process.
fingerprint.solved_via: craft a text file whose trailing modeline uses foldexpr with a `:source!` / `assert_fails('!cmd')` trick; when a victim (often a cron/mail-driven user) opens it in a vulnerable Vim, the command runs as them. A phishing/second-user step.
fingerprint.technique: a file's modeline sets fen/fde so opening it runs an expression (source!)

summary: Vim/Neovim before 8.1.1365 execute a modeline's fold expression on file open, so a booby-trapped text file is code execution as whoever opens it — a lateral/second-user step against a user who reviews dropped files.
title: Vim/Neovim — modeline arbitrary code execution (CVE-2019-12735)

fingerprint.detection: cache keys/values carrying a Marshal signature (\x04\x08) from user input, and a ruby worker spawning a shell shortly after a cache read.
fingerprint.solved_via: where the app passes attacker-influenced values into Rails.cache / a raw cache write, the value is Marshal-loaded on read; a serialized universal gadget becomes RCE. Source review (often via a leaked git repo) confirms the sink and version.
fingerprint.technique: user-controlled data reaches Marshal.load through the cache store, deserialising

summary: Rails <=6.0.3 can pass untrusted data into Marshal.load via the cache store, so an app that caches user-influenced values under the vulnerable path is deserialisation RCE — usually found by reading the app's source first.
title: Ruby on Rails — unsafe Marshal in cache/cookie store (CVE-2020-8165)

fingerprint.detection: a GET to /bin/get/Main/SolrSearch (or the REST search) whose media/query carries 'groovy' or Runtime.exec, and a java process spawning a shell.
fingerprint.solved_via: request the SolrSearch endpoint with a payload in the search text that XWiki renders as a Groovy script (async/groovy macro), executing as the wiki user with no login. URL-encode the expression; the version gates it.
fingerprint.technique: the SolrSearch macro evaluates a Groovy expression from an unauthenticated query

summary: XWiki up to 15.10.11 evaluates a Groovy expression supplied to the SolrSearch macro without authentication, so a single crafted search request is RCE as the wiki user.
title: XWiki — SolrSearch unauthenticated Groovy injection (CVE-2025-24893)

fingerprint.detection: an ndsudo execution whose resolved helper lives in a world-writable directory, and a root shell parented by ndsudo.
fingerprint.solved_via: ndsudo (shipped setuid-root) execs helper binaries by name without a fixed path, so exporting a PATH with a writable dir containing a malicious 'nvme' (etc.) makes it run as root. Local privesc once you have a shell as the netdata/low user.
fingerprint.technique: the setuid ndsudo helper resolves a plugin binary by an attacker-controlled PATH

summary: Netdata's setuid ndsudo helper (<=1.45.2) resolves its helper binaries via PATH, so a writable-dir binary named like an expected helper runs as root — a clean local privilege escalation from the netdata service user.
title: Netdata — ndsudo PATH-injection privesc (CVE-2024-32019)

fingerprint.detection: rapid firejail --join invocations racing a freshly started sandbox, and a root shell parented by firejail.
fingerprint.solved_via: firejail (setuid) mishandles joining an existing sandbox: a local user races the --join path to gain a root shell in the joined namespace. Needs a local shell and firejail installed setuid; the public PoC drives the race.
fingerprint.technique: a race in firejail --join lets a user enter a sandbox as root

summary: Firejail <=0.9.68 (setuid) has a --join race that yields a root shell in the joined namespace — a local privilege escalation wherever firejail is installed setuid.
title: Firejail — --join namespace privilege escalation (CVE-2022-31214)

fingerprint.detection: a SAML response POST to the ManageEngine ACS endpoint from an unexpected client, and the product's Java process spawning a shell.
fingerprint.solved_via: when SAML SSO is configured, the bundled vulnerable xmlsec accepts a crafted SAML response, and the product deserialises/executes into RCE as the service account. The public exploit needs the SAML endpoint and the issuer URL.
fingerprint.technique: an outdated Apache xmlsec lets a forged SAML response reach unauthenticated RCE

summary: Many ManageEngine products (SAML SSO enabled) bundle a vulnerable xmlsec, so a forged SAML response is unauthenticated RCE as the service account — a foothold on an enterprise management app off a single HTTPS port.
title: ManageEngine (ADSelfService/ServiceDesk) — SAML pre-auth RCE (CVE-2022-47966)

fingerprint.detection: a POST to /sqleditor/query_tool/download carrying Python syntax in the parameter, and a shell child of the pgAdmin (python) process.
fingerprint.solved_via: the /sqleditor/query_tool/download and query-commit endpoints pass an attacker-controlled value into a Python eval, so an authenticated pgAdmin user runs code on the pgAdmin host. Needs a pgAdmin login — leaked/reused DB-tool creds supply it.
fingerprint.technique: unsanitised parameters to the Query Tool endpoints reach Python eval

summary: pgAdmin 4 <=9.1 evaluates an unsanitised Query Tool parameter as Python, so an authenticated user achieves RCE on the pgAdmin host — a step that pairs with any leaked pgAdmin/DB credential.
title: pgAdmin 4 — Query Tool POST parameter RCE (CVE-2025-2945)

fingerprint.detection: outbound CONNECT/GET through the proxy to RFC1918 destinations from an external client, and internal services seeing the proxy's source IP.
fingerprint.solved_via: an exposed Squid on 3128 (or one whose creds you recovered) will proxy requests to internal services and, via CONNECT, tunnel arbitrary TCP — enumerate the internal range through it and reach ports the perimeter blocks. A pivot, not an exploit.
fingerprint.technique: an open or credentialed Squid relays your traffic to hosts it can reach but you cannot

summary: A reachable Squid proxy on 3128 becomes a pivot: proxy HTTP to internal hosts and CONNECT-tunnel other TCP through it, scanning and reaching services the perimeter hides — the entry technique on proxy-fronted networks.
title: Squid proxy (3128) — CONNECT/port-bounce into the internal network

fingerprint.detection: a GET to the HFS root with %00 and a '{.exec' / '{.save' macro in the query, and a child process (cmd/powershell) parented by the HFS binary.
fingerprint.solved_via: HFS's findMacroMarker regex mishandles %00, so a search query like '?search=%00{.exec|cmd.}' is parsed as a server macro and runs the command as the HFS user (Windows). searchsploit rejetto, or hit /?search= by hand; version-exact.
fingerprint.technique: a null byte in the search parameter smuggles an HFS macro that executes commands

summary: Rejetto HttpFileServer 2.3 (a Windows file-sharing web server, often on 80/8080) treats a %00-prefixed search value as a macro, so '{.exec|...}' is unauthenticated command execution. Confirm the exact version from the HFS banner first.
title: Rejetto HttpFileServer 2.3 — null-byte macro RCE (CVE-2014-6287)

fingerprint.detection: a PROPFIND to '/' with an oversized 'If:' header containing '<http://...>' twice, and a shell spawned by w3wp.exe / the IIS worker.
fingerprint.solved_via: IIS 6.0's WebDAV (Windows Server 2003) has a buffer overflow in ScStoragePathFromUrl reached through a PROPFIND with a long 'If:' header carrying two http:// URLs — 'ExplodingCan'. metasploit iis_webdav_scstoragepathfromurl, or the public PoC; RCE as the IIS worker. Confirm WebDAV is enabled (davtest).
fingerprint.technique: an over-long crafted If: header overflows ScStoragePathFromUrl in the WebDAV service

summary: IIS 6.0 (Server 2003) with WebDAV enabled is remotely exploitable via the ScStoragePathFromUrl overflow — a versioned-service foothold: fingerprint IIS 6.0, confirm WebDAV, then ExplodingCan for a worker-context shell.
title: Microsoft IIS 6.0 WebDAV — ScStoragePathFromUrl overflow (CVE-2017-7269)

fingerprint.detection: a GET to the Icinga Web 2 static/font/js route containing '../' reading outside the asset dir, then a resource/navigation config write pointing at a PHP path.
fingerprint.solved_via: CVE-2022-24716 lets an UNAUTHENTICATED request to the static library route read arbitrary files (icingaweb2 config, /etc/passwd, API/DB creds); with the creds it leaks, CVE-2022-24715 abuses an SSH-resource / custom-navigation config write to plant a PHP file and execute — RCE as the web user. Version-gated to <=2.9.5.
fingerprint.technique: a static-asset path traversal reads server files; a resource config then reaches RCE

summary: Icinga Web 2 <=2.9.5 exposes an unauthenticated arbitrary file read via its static asset route (CVE-2022-24716) — harvest its own config + creds — and then an authenticated resource-config RCE (CVE-2022-24715). A monitoring-service foothold.
title: Icinga Web 2 — unauth file disclosure then authed RCE (CVE-2022-24716/-24715)

fingerprint.detection: a request to /q with a metric/yrange param carrying backticks / 'system(' / shell metacharacters, and a child process parented by the OpenTSDB (java) process.
fingerprint.solved_via: OpenTSDB's /q graph endpoint passes params (yrange, y2range, key, etc.) into a generated Gnuplot script without sanitising; a value containing 'system("...")' or a shell metacharacter runs as the OpenTSDB user. Unauthenticated on 4242/tcp; version-gated to <=2.4.0.
fingerprint.technique: unsanitised query params flow into a Gnuplot script the server runs, injecting a command

summary: OpenTSDB <=2.4.0 (a time-series DB usually on 4242/tcp) injects unsanitised /q graph parameters into a Gnuplot script it executes, so a crafted param is unauthenticated RCE — a data-service foothold, not a web-app bug.
title: OpenTSDB — Gnuplot parameter injection RCE (CVE-2020-35476)

fingerprint.detection: a POST to the SQLPad connection-test/create endpoint whose fields contain '{{' and 'child_process' / 'process.mainModule', and a shell child of the node process.
fingerprint.solved_via: SQLPad renders connection fields (the database/schema/driver values) through nunjucks server-side; an unauthenticated connection-test with a '{{ ... process ... child_process.exec ... }}' payload executes as the SQLPad user. Version-gated to <6.10.1.
fingerprint.technique: a connection field is rendered as a nunjucks template, so {{ }} reaches child_process

summary: SQLPad <=6.10.0 (a web SQL editor) renders connection fields as nunjucks templates, so an unauthenticated connection test carrying a template payload is RCE — a versioned service foothold that a leaked/guessed instance on any port exposes.
title: SQLPad — connection-test template injection RCE (CVE-2022-0944)

fingerprint.detection: POSTs to 59777/tcp with a JSON body naming getDeviceInfo / listFiles / getFile from an unexpected host — the app has no auth on this port at all.
fingerprint.solved_via: ES File Explorer starts an HTTP server on tcp/59777 on the Android device; anyone on the network POSTs JSON commands (getDeviceInfo, listFiles, listPics, getFile) with no auth to enumerate and pull files off the phone. Version-gated to <4.1.9.7.4.
fingerprint.technique: the app opens an unauthenticated HTTP server on 59777 that answers JSON file commands

summary: ES File Explorer <4.1.9.7.4 exposes an unauthenticated control server on tcp/59777 of the Android device, so a JSON command reads arbitrary files and device metadata over the LAN — a mobile/IoT service foothold that a full-port scan reveals.
title: ES File Explorer (Android) — open HTTP server file read (CVE-2019-6447)

fingerprint.detection: an inbound request carrying an 'x-middleware-subrequest' header reaching a route whose access control lives in middleware — legitimate clients never send it.
fingerprint.solved_via: Next.js uses the internal 'x-middleware-subrequest' header to avoid recursive middleware runs; sending it on an external request (value naming the middleware path, e.g. 'middleware' or a repeated 'src/middleware') makes the framework SKIP middleware entirely — so any authentication/authorization implemented there is bypassed. Affects <14.2.25 and 15.x <15.2.3 (and the 11-13 line).
fingerprint.technique: the x-middleware-subrequest header makes Next.js skip middleware, bypassing its auth

summary: Next.js apps that enforce auth in middleware are bypassable by adding the 'x-middleware-subrequest' header, which tells the framework the request is an internal subrequest and skips middleware — reaching protected routes unauthenticated. Keyed to the Next.js version.
title: Next.js — middleware authorization bypass (CVE-2025-29927)

fingerprint.detection: a POST to the Strapi admin password-reset with no valid token, then a plugin-install request whose parameter carries a shell metacharacter, and a shell child of node.
fingerprint.solved_via: Strapi (3.0.0-beta.17.x and earlier) lets an UNAUTHENTICATED request to the admin password-reset set a new admin password (CVE-2019-18818); as admin, the plugin install / content-type builder passes a value into a shell command (CVE-2019-19609) for RCE as the Strapi user. Fingerprint Strapi from its /admin and _health routes.
fingerprint.technique: an unauth admin password reset takes the account; a plugin-install param then injects a command

summary: Strapi (headless CMS) before ~3.0.0-beta.17.5 allows an unauthenticated admin password reset (CVE-2019-18818) which chains into an authenticated command injection (CVE-2019-19609) — a CMS-service foothold to RCE. Confirm Strapi from /admin first.
title: Strapi — unauth password reset then authed RCE (CVE-2019-18818/-19609)

summary: The SaaS-specific slice of broken object-level authorization: whether one tenant/organization can reach another tenant's data or actions. Distinct from generic IDOR in that the boundary under test is the TENANT, and the highest-value tests use a two-account (tenant A vs tenant B) setup plus header/claim scoping abuse. Lead with this on any multi-tenant SaaS target.
title: Cross-Tenant / Multi-Tenant Access-Control Testing

summary: User-configurable webhooks are a rich, under-tested SaaS surface. The server makes an outbound request to a URL the user controls, making webhooks a first-class SSRF primitive; the shared signing secret and its verification are also frequently mishandled. Test the outbound side (SSRF/metadata), the secret side (leakage, weak/optional signatures), and delivery (replay).
title: Webhook Security Testing (SSRF, Secret Leakage, Signature Bypass, Replay)

summary: OWASP API5:2023. Where BOLA is about objects, BFLA is about ACTIONS: a low-privileged or regular user invoking administrative or higher-role FUNCTIONS (create-user, change-role, delete-tenant, export-all, feature-flags). The gap is an endpoint that checks authentication but not the caller's ROLE. Test by taking privileged calls captured as an admin and replaying them as a normal user, and by guessing admin routes/verbs.
title: Broken Function-Level Authorization (BFLA / Privileged-Function Access)

summary: Many apps trust the Host header (or X-Forwarded-Host) to build absolute URLs, route requests, or key caches. Tampering with it enables password-reset poisoning (reset link points to attacker), web cache poisoning, routing-based SSRF to internal vhosts, and occasional authentication/ACL bypasses. Always test both the real Host header and the X-Forwarded-* family.
title: HTTP Host Header Attacks (Reset Poisoning, Routing SSRF, Cache Poisoning)

summary: Encoding, packing and command-line mangling change what a payload LOOKS like without changing what it DOES. Detection therefore moves from the string to the shape: the encoding itself is the signal, and the payload has to decode before it can run.
title: Obfuscation — how it works and how it is detected

summary: Running code without writing it to disk defeats file-based scanning and forensics that start from the filesystem. It does not defeat process, memory or network telemetry — which is exactly where detection for this family lives.
title: In-memory execution — how it works and how it is detected

summary: Running code inside another process borrows that process's identity and trust. The cross-process operations required to do it are rare, well-instrumented, and among the highest-fidelity detections available on Windows.
title: Process injection — how it works and how it is detected

summary: Interfering with the sensors themselves — the scan interface and the event pipeline — is tracked by ATT&CK as Defense Impairment. It is loud in a specific way: the SILENCE is the signal, and turning a sensor off is itself an event.
title: AMSI / ETW tampering — how it works and how it is detected

summary: Using signed, built-in system binaries to do the work means nothing unusual is installed and nothing fails an allowlist. Detection shifts entirely from WHAT ran to HOW it ran — the parent, the arguments, and what it did next.
title: Living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) — how it works and how it is detected

summary: Deciding not to act — because the environment looks like a sandbox, or because acting slowly stays under a threshold — targets the analysis pipeline rather than the sensor. The checks themselves are observable, and thresholds are a defender's choice, not a law.
title: Behavioural evasion (sandbox, timing, environment checks) — how it works and how it is detected

summary: Encryption, protocol mimicry, domain fronting and third-party services hide command-and-control CONTENT. They do not hide that a conversation happened — and metadata, not payload, is where network detection has lived for years.
title: Traffic obfuscation and covert channels — how it works and how it is detected

summary: Surviving a reboot means writing something down. Every persistence mechanism is a durable change to a small, enumerable set of places — which makes this the most detectable family on the list, and the one most worth auditing after any test.
title: Persistence — how it works and how it is detected

summary: Bug-bounty platforms publish scope changes as a dated unified diff. A wildcard added weeks or months ago is surface that, by arithmetic, almost nobody has finished testing — while the program's original scope has been ground over for years. Sort candidate targets by scope-entry AGE, newest first, and hunt there.
title: Target the Most Recently Added Wildcard (Scope-Change Diff)

summary: Program pages break resolved reports down per asset. The instinct is to hunt the asset with the most resolved reports because it 'clearly has bugs'. That is backwards: a high resolved count means the surface has been swept repeatedly and the cheap findings are gone and duplicated. Bugs correlate with UNTESTED surface, not with historical bug count.
title: Hunt Where the FEWEST Reports Have Resolved, Not the Most

summary: A Vulnerability Disclosure Program accepts reports but pays no bounty. Full-time hunters therefore skip them, so competition is low while scope is often enormous. That makes a VDP the cheapest place to convert effort into reputation and signal — which is what actually unlocks paid private programs.
title: Use VDPs to Build Signal and Earn Private Invites

summary: The gap most hunters stall in is between 'recon is done' and 'what do I actually test?'. Threat modelling is the blue-team practice that closes it: decompose the application into mechanisms, then walk each mechanism through STRIDE — Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege — and write down every attack the mechanism structurally permits. The output is a ranked list of concrete attack vectors to test by hand, instead of scanning and hoping.
title: STRIDE Threat Modelling: Turning Finished Recon Into a Test Plan

summary: The most consistently overlooked STRIDE category in bug bounty. If a user can delete, edit, or forge the log entries that record their own actions — or another user's — then the audit trail is worthless, and for a company under SOC 2 / HIPAA / PCI that is a material finding rather than a curiosity. Almost nobody tests it, which is exactly why it pays.
title: Repudiation: Attacking the Audit Trail

summary: Login is the endpoint everyone hardens: rate limits, lockout, CAPTCHA. The change-password endpoint usually is not, because the developer assumes the caller is already the account owner. When that endpoint also takes a user id from the REQUEST rather than the session, it becomes an unthrottled password oracle against any account.
title: Brute-Forcing via the Change-Password Endpoint (Rate-Limit Asymmetry)

summary: A CSRF token that EXISTS is not a CSRF token that WORKS. The common failures are not missing tokens but unbound ones: a static token that never rotates, a double-submit pair that only has to match itself, or a token validated as 'well-formed' without being tied to the session it arrived on. Each turns the control into decoration.
title: CSRF Token Binding Failures (Static, Shared, and Cross-Account Tokens)

summary: When the price, quantity, currency, or discount used to charge a customer originates from the CLIENT rather than being recomputed server-side from the catalogue, the amount charged is attacker-controlled. It is a pure business-logic flaw, needs no exotic payload, and remains common on newer e-commerce and checkout integrations.
title: Price and Amount Tampering (Client-Trusted Pricing)

summary: Applications ship entitlement decisions to the browser as booleans — hasAccessToX, isAdmin, canManage, plan tiers, feature-flag maps. Flipping them in the response reveals hidden UI instantly. The discipline that makes this worth reporting is proving the SERVER also honours the flip; a UI that unhides is not an authorization bypass.
title: Client-Trusted Feature Flags and Entitlement Booleans

summary: Protection usually lives at the CDN edge, not on the application. Any path that reaches the origin directly — a leftover origin-*/direct-*/backend-* hostname, an A record that still points at the real IP, or an IP found by certificate pivoting — serves the same application with the WAF, rate limiting and bot rules removed.
title: origin-* Hosts: Reaching the Application Behind the CDN and WAF

summary: After enumeration you hold hundreds of live hosts and can test perhaps a handful properly. The scarce resource is attention, so triage is the skill that matters most. These are cheap, high-signal observations that separate a maintained, hardened host from a forgotten one.
title: Triage Signals: Deciding Which Host Deserves Your Time

summary: Identifying the stack is not trivia — it eliminates whole categories of wasted effort and promotes others. The same test is near-worthless against one framework and high-yield against another, and knowing which is which is most of the efficiency gap between a fast hunter and a slow one.
title: Let the Framework Decide What You Test

summary: Product documentation, developer guides, role descriptions and the privacy policy are the vendor's own written statement of how the system is supposed to behave. Every sentence is a testable assertion, and any deviation is a bug you can prove against the company's own words — which makes it very hard to dispute.
title: Vendor Documentation and Policy as a Bug Oracle

summary: Single-hop pivoting is a syntax problem and every cheat sheet solves it. A chain two or three hops deep is a different problem: your box is not on the deeper networks and nothing there can route back to you, so each hop needs an outbound path AND a return path, its own SOCKS port, and tooling staged from the hop before it rather than from you. This is the discipline that holds a chain together, not the flag syntax.
title: Multi-Hop Pivot Chains — Holding a Route More Than One Hop Deep

summary: Local, remote and dynamic port forwarding are documented everywhere; which one the situation actually permits is not. Three properties decide it and none of them is preference: which way traffic is allowed to flow, whether you need one service or a whole network, and how much you are willing to leave on the compromised host. Decide in that order and the syntax question answers itself.
title: Choosing the Pivot Primitive (Direction, Shape, and Footprint)

summary: A port that does not answer has told you something about the FILTER, not about the port. Most scanning notes treat that silence as 'closed' and move on, which throws away the perimeter device as an object of enumeration and leaves you unable to say whether a service is absent or merely unreachable from where you are standing. This is how to map the filter itself: separate refused from dropped, use the scan types that report reachability rather than port state, locate the device on the path, and only then adapt the scan to what that device does not inspect.
title: Reading a Packet Filter — ACL Enumeration and Scan-Time Evasion

summary: On an IT network the scan is reconnaissance and the exploit is the risk. On an OT segment the SCAN is the risk. Controllers run tiny embedded TCP stacks with a handful of connection slots and no expectation of being probed, and a default nmap invocation faults them often enough that it is a normal outcome rather than bad luck — the version-detection probes in particular exist to send deliberately malformed protocol traffic. A faulted PLC is not a ticket; it is a stopped process and potentially a safety event. This is the discipline that lets you enumerate one anyway.
title: Scanning an ICS/OT Segment Without Knocking It Over
